subject: Ohno et al. (2002)
object: Ohno et al. (2002) identified 3 recessive rapsyn (RAPSN) mutations in 4 patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency who had no mutations in AChR-subunit genes. One patient carried L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3, 2 were homozygous for N88K, and 1 carried N88K and 553ins5, a frameshift in TPR5.

subject: RAPSN p.N88K
object: RAPSN

subject: Ohno et al. (2002)
object: Ohno et al. (2002) found an L14P missense mutation in tetratricopeptide repeat 1 (TPR1) of rapsyn (RAPSN). It was in the compound heterozygous state with N88K in a patient with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency.

subject: RAPSN p.L14P
object: RAPSN

subject: Ohno et al. (2002)
object: Ohno et al. (2002) found a 553ins5 insertion in rapsyn (RAPSN) that causes a frameshift in TPR5. It was in the compound heterozygous state with N88K in a patient with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency.

subject: RAPSN c.553ins5
object: RAPSN

subject: Ohno et al. (2002)
object: Ohno et al. (2002) performed endplate studies in each of the 4 patients with RAPSN mutations. These showed decreased staining for rapsyn and AChR and impaired postsynaptic morphological development.

subject: Ohno et al. (2002)
object: Ohno et al. (2002) expressed the mutant rapsyn proteins in HEK cells. None of the 3 mutations hindered rapsyn self-association, but all 3 reduced coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

subject: Ohno et al. (2003)
object: Ohno et al. (2003) identified a -27C-G mutation in the RAPSN promoter region in a patient with congenital myasthenic syndrome (patient 1). The mutation changes an E-box at -27 to -22 from CAGCTG to GAGCTG, and the allele harboring it was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. Position +1 was the major transcriptional start site, determined to be 172 nucleotides upstream of the translational start site.

subject: RAPSN -27C-->G
object: RAPSN

subject: Ohno et al. (2003)
object: Ohno et al. (2003) identified a -38A-G mutation in the RAPSN promoter region in 7 patients (patients 2-8) with congenital myasthenic syndrome, all of Oriental Jewish stock of Iraqi or Iranian origin. The mutation changes an E-box at -40 to -35 from CAACTG to CAGCTG, which does not affect the consensus CANNTG sequence.

subject: RAPSN -38A-->G
object: RAPSN

subject: Ohno et al. (2003)
object: Ohno et al. (2003) reported that the 7 congenital myasthenic syndrome patients of Oriental Jewish Iraqi or Iranian origin carrying the RAPSN -38A-G promoter mutation had facial malformations.

subject: Ohno et al. (2003)
object: Ohno et al. (2003) showed by haplotype analysis that the RAPSN -38A-G promoter mutation in Oriental Jewish patients of Iraqi or Iranian origin arose from a common founder.

subject: Ohno et al. (2003)
object: In electrophoretic mobility shift assays, Ohno et al. (2003) found that the RAPSN -38A-G mutation gained, and -27C-G lost, binding affinity for different components of C2C12 myotube nuclear extracts. In luciferase reporter assays, both mutations attenuated reporter expression in C2C12 myotubes. The -27C-G mutation also attenuated expression in HEK cells transfected with MyoD or myogenin, and it markedly attenuated the enhancer activity of an E-box on an SV40 promoter. The authors concluded that impaired RAPSN promoter activity predicts reduced rapsyn expression and endplate acetylcholine receptor deficiency.

subject: Dunne and Maselli (2003)
object: Dunne and Maselli (2003) described 4 patients from 4 unrelated families with congenital myasthenic syndrome and RAPSN mutations. In 2 cases the diagnosis was confirmed by microelectrode and electron microscopy studies. The patient homozygous for N88K was only mildly affected, and the 3 compound heterozygous patients were severely affected.

subject: Dunne and Maselli (2003)
object: Dunne and Maselli (2003) found the RAPSN N88K mutation in all 4 patients with CMS from 4 families: 1 patient was homozygous and 3 were compound heterozygous with a second RAPSN mutation. N88K lies within the putative leucine zipper motif, which may be important for AChR clustering.

subject: Dunne and Maselli (2003)
object: Dunne and Maselli (2003) found a RAPSN L14P mutation together with N88K in a severely affected compound heterozygous patient with CMS. The authors predicted that L14P causes a conformational change at the N terminus that may disrupt membrane association.

subject: Dunne and Maselli (2003)
object: Dunne and Maselli (2003) found a RAPSN 46insC mutation together with N88K in a severely affected compound heterozygous patient with CMS. The authors predicted that 46insC truncates the protein.

subject: RAPSN c.46insc
object: RAPSN

subject: Dunne and Maselli (2003)
object: Dunne and Maselli (2003) found a RAPSN Y269X nonsense mutation together with N88K in a severely affected compound heterozygous patient with CMS. The authors predicted that Y269X truncates the protein.

subject: RAPSN p.Y269*
object: RAPSN

subject: Dunne and Maselli (2003)
object: Dunne and Maselli (2003) observed that the patient homozygous for the RAPSN N88K mutation was mildly affected. The 3 compound heterozygous patients, who carried N88K with L14P, 46insC, or Y269X, were severely affected. The authors suggested that the predicted effects of these second mutations may explain the severe disease in the compound heterozygotes.

subject: Müller et al. (2003)
object: Müller et al. (2003) screened 120 patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome from 110 unrelated families for the RAPSN N88K mutation by restriction fragment length polymorphism and sequence analysis, and identified N88K in 12 patients from 10 independent families, either in homozygous state or in compound heterozygous state with another missense mutation.

subject: Müller et al. (2003)
object: Müller et al. (2003) reported that in 12 CMS patients with RAPSN N88K, symptoms usually began perinatally or in the first years of life, although 1 patient had no myasthenic symptoms before the third decade. Typical features included bilateral ptosis, weakness of facial, bulbar, and limb muscles, and frequent crisis-like exacerbations with respiratory insufficiency provoked by stress, fever, or infections in early childhood. Patients generally had mild to moderate myasthenic symptoms, but severity and onset varied greatly.

subject: Müller et al. (2003)
object: Müller et al. (2003) found that patients with RAPSN N88K showed a favorable response to anticholinesterase treatment.

subject: Müller et al. (2003)
object: Müller et al. (2003) found that all RAPSN N88K families originated from Central or Western European countries, and genotype analysis indicated derivation from a common founder; they concluded that N88K is a frequent cause of rapsyn-related CMS in European patients.

subject: Richard et al. (2003)
object: Richard et al. (2003) suggested a possible founder effect for the rapsyn (RAPSN) N88K mutation in patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome.

subject: Richard et al. (2003)
object: Richard et al. (2003) identified novel rapsyn (RAPSN) mutations in patients with congenital myasthenic syndromes.

subject: Burke et al. (2003)
object: Burke et al. (2003) identified rapsyn (RAPSN) mutations in 16 unrelated patients with congenital/hereditary myasthenic syndrome. All 16 patients carried the N88K mutation.

subject: Burke et al. (2003)
object: Burke et al. (2003) described two distinct phenotypes among 16 patients with RAPSN-related congenital myasthenic syndrome: early onset and late onset. The early-onset form was often associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and life-threatening crises. The late-onset form developed in adolescence or adulthood and was at first mistaken for seronegative myasthenia gravis.

subject: Burke et al. (2003)
object: Burke et al. (2003) noted that the late-onset RAPSN phenotype can be mistaken for seronegative myasthenia gravis, and that recognizing it should prevent inappropriate immunotherapy.

subject: Yasaki et al. (2004)
object: Yasaki et al. (2004) reported a 28-year-old French man with congenital myasthenic syndrome who had had mild diplopia and fatigability since age 5 years. His muscle biopsy showed a marked reduction in rapsyn and acetylcholine receptor (AChR) at neuromuscular junctions, as well as a simplified subneural apparatus.

subject: Yasaki et al. (2004)
object: In a French patient with congenital myasthenic syndrome and AChR deficiency, Yasaki et al. (2004) ruled out mutations in the AChR subunit genes and found a homozygous N88K mutation in the RAPSN gene. Cell expression studies had previously shown that this mutation impairs aggregation of rapsyn and AChR at the neuromuscular junction.

subject: Yasaki et al. (2004)
object: Yasaki et al. (2004) found the RAPSN N88K mutation in the heterozygous state in 5 of 300 unrelated control subjects. They concluded that the mutation is not infrequent in the healthy population.

subject: Yasaki et al. (2004)
object: Yasaki et al. (2004) performed electrophysiological studies on biopsied intercostal muscle from a patient homozygous for the RAPSN N88K mutation. They found that the fatigable weakness reflected both reduced AChR density in the membrane and a decline in endplate potentials evoked at low frequency.

subject: Dunne and Maselli (2004)
object: Dunne and Maselli (2004) used 7 intragenic SNPs spanning 8 kb of the RAPSN gene to characterize the haplotype associated with the N88K mutation. In 3 affected N88K homozygotes, they identified a common haplotype that was present in all heterozygous carriers of N88K, supporting a founder effect.

subject: Dunne and Maselli (2004)
object: Dunne and Maselli (2004) found that 2 asymptomatic individuals homozygous for the RAPSN N88K mutation carried a second haplotype that differed at 3 SNP sites downstream of the mutation. The authors suggested that recombination events may have occurred within the rapsyn gene and that this may have implications for phenotypic expression of the disease.

subject: Müller et al. (2004)
object: Müller et al. (2004) described a German patient with sporadic congenital myasthenic syndrome of early onset associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, recurrent episodes of respiratory insufficiency provoked by infections, and moderate general weakness responsive to anticholinesterase treatment.

subject: Müller et al. (2004)
object: In a sporadic German patient with CMS, Müller et al. (2004) used RFLP, long-range PCR and sequence analysis to identify compound heterozygosity for the RAPSN N88K mutation and a large deletion of about 4.5 kb disrupting the RAPSN gene.

subject: RAPSN large deletion of about 4.5 kb disrupting the RAPSN gene
object: RAPSN

subject: Müller et al. (2004)
object: Müller et al. (2004) suggested that the RAPSN 4.5-kb deletion may have been caused by Alu-mediated unequal homologous recombination and hypothesized that numerous interspersed Alu elements may predispose the RAPSN locus to genetic rearrangements.

subject: Maselli et al. (2007)
object: Maselli et al. (2007) reported congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by two rapsyn (RAPSN) mutations other than N88K.

subject: Michalk et al. (2008)
object: Michalk et al. (2008) identified novel recessive missense mutations in RAPSN in patients with fetal akinesia deformation sequence (FADS) disorders. These mutations caused a severe but not necessarily lethal phenotype, whereas homozygous nonsense mutations in CHRNA1 and CHRND were lethal.

subject: Michalk et al. (2008)
object: Michalk et al. (2008) concluded that complete or severe functional disruption of fetal AChR causes lethal multiple pterygium syndrome, whereas milder alterations result in fetal hypokinesia with inborn contractures or a myasthenic syndrome later in life.

subject: Michalk et al. (2008)
object: Michalk et al. (2008) studied Rapsn and the AChR subunit genes in mouse embryos. Expression was found in skeletal muscles and also in early somite development. The authors suggested that early developmental defects such as fetal edema, cystic hygroma, or cardiac defects might be due to somite expression, in addition to muscle-specific effects.

subject: Milone et al. (2009)
object: Milone et al. (2009) reported clinical, electrophysiologic, pathologic, and molecular studies in 39 patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome due to rapsyn defects. In all but 1 patient, the disease presented in the first 2 years of life. Nine patients had constant or episodic ophthalmoparesis, 1 patient had a pure limb-girdle phenotype, and more than half had intermittent exacerbations.

subject: Milone et al. (2009)
object: Milone et al. (2009) had long-term follow-up for 25 patients after the start of cholinergic therapy: 21 became stable or improved (2 becoming asymptomatic), 3 had a progressive course, and 1 died in infancy. The authors concluded that with early diagnosis and therapy, rapsyn deficiency has a benign course in most patients.

subject: Milone et al. (2009)
object: Milone et al. (2009) found in 7 patients who had endplate studies that the average AChR count per endplate and the synaptic response to ACh were less reduced than in patients with low-expressor AChR mutations.

subject: Milone et al. (2009)
object: Among 39 patients with rapsyn-deficient congenital myasthenic syndrome, Milone et al. (2009) found that 8 were homozygous and 23 heterozygous for the common N88K mutation in the RAPSN gene. Homozygosity for N88K was associated with varying grades of severity.

subject: Milone et al. (2009)
object: Milone et al. (2009) identified 6 novel RAPSN mutations in their cohort, comprising 3 missense mutations, an in-frame deletion, a splice-site mutation, and a nonsense mutation.

subject: Milone et al. (2009)
object: Milone et al. (2009) observed no genotype-phenotype correlations except in 8 Near-Eastern patients homozygous for the RAPSN promoter E-box mutation c.-38A>G, who had a mild course; this E-box mutation was associated with jaw deformities.
